BUILD: the core of the prompt wizard. A researched plan for it already exists as cards on the project board — read them first, they contain the reasoning and you should follow it rather than re-deciding.

## Read the plan
The board is SQLite at `C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Kodely\Kodely Board\board.sqlite` (`node:sqlite`, `DatabaseSync`). **READ ONLY — never write to it.** Tables: `boards(id,name,position)`, `columns(id,boardId,name,position)`, `cards(id,columnId,title,description,...)`. Board id `720aa8c1-d259-4e49-b777-c58965efabd1`, column named `Prompt Wizard` — 37 cards. Read every description, not just titles.

## Build steps 1, 2 and 4 only
**Explicitly NOT step 3** (logo upload, current-site import, reference-site fetch). Those need SSRF mitigation and an out-of-band logo path; leave them for a later pass and do not stub them in a way that implies they work.

The plan's own principles, which are non-negotiable:
- **A side door on the composer, never a gate.** The raw prompt box stays the default. Nothing may sit between someone and typing.
- **The wizard emits a PROMPT, not a config object.** Its output is text a human can read and edit.
- **Colour is expressed as exact hexes plus a catalogue preset id, never as adjectives.** "Warm and modern" produces the generic look this exists to kill.
- **The signed-out wizard makes ZERO model calls.** Assembly is local string work.
- Step 4 lands in the composer textarea and reuses the existing Enhance/Revert affordance rather than inventing a second review UI.

## Ground truth to read before writing anything
- `lib/enhance.ts` + `app/api/enhance/route.ts` — Enhance already exists. The wizard assembles, Enhance polishes; neither duplicates the other.
- `lib/templates.ts` + `app/templates/` — 23 template prompts. Same relationship: complement, don't duplicate.
- `components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx` — the composer, the image path, and how Enhance is surfaced.
- `lib/pending-prompt.ts` — how a prompt survives signup. There is a board card warning about sessionStorage size limits; heed it.
- `lib/assets/patterns.ts` — 30 curated gradients and palettes already exist with stable ids. **Use them as the catalogue** rather than inventing a second colour vocabulary.
- `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM — what the builder can actually do, and its rules against inventing business facts and against controls that only pretend to work.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `app/wizard/**`, `components/wizard/**`, `lib/wizard.ts`
Do NOT edit `components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx`, `lib/pending-prompt.ts`, `lib/agent.ts`, `lib/assets/**`, `app/templates/**` or anything else. If the hand-off genuinely needs a change outside your scope, describe the exact edit in your report instead of making it.

## Constraints
- Match the marketing idiom: read `app/templates/page.tsx` and `app/pricing/page.tsx`. `rounded-2xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, restrained, monochrome with the brand gradient only as an accent.
- **No new white text on the brand gradient** — it fails contrast (worst 1.81:1), a known accepted issue.
- Accessibility bar, matching the recent pass: `SkipLink` + `<main id="main-content" tabIndex={-1}>`, real `<label>`s, a genuine `fieldset`/`legend` radio group for the look picker, visible `focus-visible:` states, `role="status"` for step changes, keyboard operable throughout, no horizontal scroll at 380px.
- Every wizard step must be skippable and the whole thing abandonable at any point.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must BOTH be clean — currently ZERO errors and ZERO warnings. Keep it exactly there.**

## Report back
Which board cards you implemented and which you deliberately deferred, the exact assembled-prompt format with a real example, how colour reaches the model, the hand-off mechanism, anything you need outside your scope, and what you verified.

1	===== [0] Wizard is a side door on the composer, never a gate =====
2	The board already says 'never force the wizard'. Make that structural rather than a promise: PromptHero keeps the raw textarea as the mounted default, and the wizard opens in-place from one small link under the box ('Not sure what to write?'). Nothing about the wizard's existence changes the raw path — same textarea, same send button, same Enter-to-submit. A 'Skip to the box' control is visible on every wizard screen and returns whatever has been assembled so far into the textarea, so abandoning halfway is a productive action rather than a loss. Two rules follow from this and should be enforced in review: (1) the wizard never blocks the send button, and (2) the wizard never renders on first paint — a returning power user must not see it at all. Precedent worth noting: Lovable's design-guidance step is auto-skipped when the prompt already specifies fonts/colours/branding (docs.lovable.dev/features/design-guidance), i.e. even the vendor that pushes hardest on an up-front design step gets out of the way for users who don't need it.
3	
4	===== [1] The wizard emits a prompt, not a config object =====
5	The single architectural decision the rest of this epic depends on. Every wizard answer must be serialised into plain English inside the composer textarea, not held in a hidden state blob that /api/generate reads. Three reasons. First, it is the only design that honours 'raw box stays the default' at the level of the data model — the wizard's output is literally a raw-box prompt, so there is exactly one build path to test, debug and eval. Second, it keeps the user in control: they can read what the wizard decided on their behalf and delete the half they disagree with, which a hidden config cannot offer. Third, lib/templates.ts already proves the shape works — the 23 template prompts are exactly what an expert-written wizard output looks like (audience, tone, ordered sections, bracketed placeholders), so the wizard's job is to help someone produce one of those, not to invent a parallel format. The only exceptions are the artefacts that genuinely cannot be text: the logo bytes and any attached image. Those travel out of band (see the logo and image-slot cards).
6	
7	===== [2] Step 1 — what and who, the only required screen =====
8	One screen: category chips reusing the seven TEMPLATE_CATEGORIES from lib/templates.ts plus 'something else'; an optional site/business name; and one free-text line answering 'what do you actually do'. Picking a category loads the matching template prompt from lib/templates.ts as the skeleton the later steps fill in — that is the whole reason the gallery and the wizard are one feature and not two, and it means the wizard inherits 23 hand-written prompts' worth of guardrails (no fake booking form, link-outs instead of backends, bracketed placeholders) for free. Keep the name optional: someone who has not named the business yet must not be stuck on screen one, and the never-invent-facts rule already handles the gap with [your business name]. Everything after this screen is skippable, so the honest minimum path through the wizard is one screen plus review.
9	
10	===== [3] Step 2 — pick a look from six pre-rendered directions =====
11	Lovable shows three rendered design directions before the first build and lets you refine the chosen one up to six times; it costs no extra credits because it rides the normal chat (docs.lovable.dev/features/design-guidance). Kodely cannot copy that literally — a rendered preview here means a real build at 144-472 credits. But we can get most of the value for zero model cost, because lib/assets/patterns.ts already ships a curated gradient catalogue with named families (warm, cool, vivid, nature, neutral, pastel, dark) and real hexes. Render six direction cards purely in CSS from those presets — each card is a gradient, a type scale and a density, with a human name ('Warm and rustic', 'Clean and clinical', 'Bold and editorial') — and let the user pick one. No model call, no network, instant, and the choice resolves to concrete hexes and a preset id rather than an adjective. This screen is the cheapest and highest-leverage of the four hard inputs and should ship first.

The file says so itself: taste needs a judge, and a judge is a different, more expensive instrument. Treat the deterministic score as a regression gate, not as the verdict.
102	
103	===== [34] A pairwise judge for the question the static score cannot answer =====
104	The honest measure of the wizard is 'does the site look better', and nothing in the current harness measures that. The instrument that fits is a pairwise judge: render both builds of a paired fixture, show a model both screenshots with the original business brief and ask which one a real owner would rather publish, with the order randomised to control position bias and each pair judged a few times to get a rate rather than a verdict. Design notes that matter more than the prompt: judge on rendered screenshots rather than source, because the source is what the generator optimised for; use a different model from the builder; and keep the rubric short and concrete (does it look designed for this business, is the palette specific, is there one distinctive idea) so it maps onto the quality bar in lib/agent.ts rather than to generic taste. This is a genuinely new instrument with its own cost and its own failure modes, so it deserves to be scoped as a separate piece of work rather than bolted onto score.mjs, which is explicit about being deterministic, offline and model-free.
105	
106	===== [35] Guardrail metric: credits per first build must not quietly inflate =====
107	A wizard makes prompts longer, and a longer prompt is not free: it is input tokens on every one of up to 8 agent turns, and it tends to ask for more sections, which is more output tokens again. Measured first builds already span 144 to 472 credits, a 3x spread across two samples, so a wizard that adds 30% to the mean would be invisible in that noise while quietly eating a third of the 750-credit signup grant. Track credits per first build as a guardrail alongside whatever the wizard improves, with an explicit trade rule agreed before the experiment runs rather than after: a materially higher first-build rating or publish rate justifies a modest cost increase, a flat rating at higher cost does not. The eval harness reports imputed credits per fixture already, so the paired fixtures give an offline read before any user sees it. Related and worth fixing alongside: estimateCredits is still a two-sample guess and the comment in lib/credits.ts asks for real percentiles from a full eval sweep — the wizard experiment is a good reason to finally run one.
108	
109	===== [36] Competitor onboarding: what four AI builders actually ask before the first build =====
110	Verified from vendor docs, August 2026. Lovable: freeform box, no wizard, but a design-guidance step shows three rendered design directions on a first UI request, refinable up to six times, auto-skipped when the prompt already specifies fonts/colours/branding, and adds no credit cost. Its documented reference-URL path is the Build-with-URL API, where an html= parameter takes a publicly accessible page that Lovable fetches server-side and uses for layout, content and styling, with up to 10 combined image and page references (docs.lovable.dev, changelog dates html= to Jun 2026). Bolt: prompt box, Build now, auth, a post-signup survey, then a build — no design step, but it has the closest thing to this epic in production: an Enhance-prompt dialog that asks the user a set of questions and then generates a recommended prompt they can edit (support.bolt.new/building/using-bolt/interacting-ai). Public websites are accepted only as a design-system source, on paid Team plans, taking 45-60 minutes. v0: leanest of all, sign in, new chat, prompt; no design picker and no reference-URL feature at all — screenshot upload is the documented way to replicate a design (v0.app/docs/screenshots). Base44: the richest entry surface, with Start-from-URL offering an explicit Content-and-Design vs Design-only choice, a real credentialed migration path for an existing app, a dedicated logo slot in the dashboard, and a brand kit that can be built from a website URL and is preselected so the first prompt already matches. Two corrections to received wisdom: Lovable has no documented prompt-enhance feature and neither does v0 — Bolt is the one with the questionnaire.

513	/** FNV-1a. Small, stable, and good enough to spread names across a hue wheel. */
514	function hash(input: string): number {
515	  let h = 0x811c9dc5;
516	  for (let i = 0; i < input.length; i++) {
517	    h ^= input.charCodeAt(i);
518	    h = Math.imul(h, 0x01000193) >>> 0;
519	  }
520	  return h;
521	}

523	/** Up to two initials: "Ada Lovelace" -> "AL", "cheryl" -> "C". */
524	export function initialsOf(name: string): string {
525	  const words = name.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
526	  if (words.length === 0) return "?";
527	  if (words.length === 1) return words[0].slice(0, 2).toUpperCase();
528	  return (words[0][0] + words[words.length - 1][0]).toUpperCase();
529	}

535	 * are fixed so every avatar in a list has the same weight — only the hue moves.
536	 */
537	export function avatarColors(name: string): AvatarColors {
538	  const h = hash(name.toLowerCase());
539	  const hue = h % 360;
540	  // Skip the 55-90deg band, where mid-lightness yellows go muddy against white text.
541	  const safeHue = hue > 55 && hue < 90 ? hue + 40 : hue;
542	  return {
543	    from: `hsl(${safeHue} 62% 52%)`,
544	    to: `hsl(${(safeHue + 28) % 360} 58% 40%)`,
545	    text: "#ffffff",
546	  };
547	}

Build a one-page website for Bloom Pilates — a reformer pilates studio in Denver.

Audience: someone who has decided to start training and is comparing two or three local studios. They want to know what a class is actually like, what it costs, and whether beginners are welcome. Tone: energetic but grown-up — motivating, not shouty.

Sections in this order:
1. Hero — the studio name, one line on what makes training here different, and a "Book your first class" button.
2. Classes — 3 or 4 class types, each with a short description, difficulty level and duration.
3. Timetable — a simple weekly grid of day / time / class. Make clear in the copy that this is the current timetable and I keep it up to date by hand.
4. Membership — 2 or 3 price options (drop-in, monthly, intro offer) as plain cards with what each includes.
5. A short "new here?" paragraph answering what to bring and how early to arrive.
6. Hours, address, footer.

Class times, prices, the address, the trainers' names and any claims about results must be bracketed placeholders — never invented.

There is no backend: no sign-up form, no payment, no class booking. The CTAs are [link to your booking system], a tel: link and a mailto: link, labelled so it is obvious where they go.

No photography available — use bold type, a high-contrast palette and inline SVG. Responsive to 380px, dark mode included.

Visual direction — I chose this, so build to it rather than picking your own. Where it disagrees with a colour or type hint earlier in this brief, this wins:
- Look: Warm and rustic. Earthy and hand-made — clay tones, serif headings, room to breathe.
- Palette: terracotta (#E2725B to #8C4A3F, 150deg). Use find_assets with the query "terracotta" to pull the exact gradient source, make those the dominant colours, and derive the rest of the palette from those hexes. Do not substitute a different colour, and do not fall back to indigo or violet.
- Typography: serif headings from the system serif stack (ui-serif, Georgia, serif) over a plain sans body, set large and unhurried.
- Density: roomy — a long vertical rhythm, roughly one idea per screen, and generous whitespace.
